analysis.one_liner: Reforms logging in Alaska's Tongass National Forest, ending guaranteed cheap timber for two pulp companies and protecting fish streams and wild lands.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 356–60, the Senate passed it 99–0, and President George H.W. Bush signed it into law as Public Law 101-626 on November 28, 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: The Tongass National Forest in Alaska had been run under special rules requiring the Forest Service to supply cheap timber to two pulp companies under 50-year contracts. This law repealed that guaranteed-supply mandate, required buffer zones where logging is banned along fish streams, protected roadless wild lands, and required annual public reports on how much money the timber program makes or loses. The final version, negotiated in a House-Senate conference, was weaker than what the House originally passed: it modified rather than terminated the pulp companies' contracts, and it cut the wilderness designations from 23 areas down to 6. It also extended a program in which the Forest Service builds logging roads for small timber purchasers.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who had been funding a timber program run to guarantee supply to two companies rather than to break even. Commercial fishermen and subsistence users, who gain protected stream buffers and wild lands that sustain salmon and wildlife. Small Alaska timber operators, who gain access to a set-aside program with Forest Service-built logging roads. Southeast Alaska communities that depend on fishing and tourism rather than pulp mills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, fishermen, and Alaska's small timber operators

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act provisions requiring appropriations to maintain the timber supply from the Tongass to dependent industry, ending the statutory guarantee of cheap public timber for two companies.
Requires buffer zones where commercial logging is prohibited along fish-bearing streams in the forest, protecting salmon habitat that supports commercial and subsistence fishing.

Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to report annually to Congress a complete analysis of the losses or gains the United States sustains on Tongass timber sales, making the program's finances public.
Requires modification of the long-term contracts with Alaska Pulp Corporation and Ketchikan Pulp Company to protect public resources and promote competition in the southeast Alaska timber industry.
Designates six wilderness areas and places additional Tongass lands under roadless Land Use Designation II management.
Prohibits construction of the Indian River–Game Creek connecting road and further efforts to connect Tenakee Springs to the Chichagof Island logging road system.

analysis.who_pays: The two pulp companies, Alaska Pulp Corporation and Ketchikan Pulp Company, which lose their guaranteed low-cost timber supply and special contract terms, and the loggers and mill workers in southeast Alaska timber towns whose jobs depended on that supply. The Forest Service must still prepare timber to meet market demand, and taxpayers continue to fund Forest Service road construction for small timber purchasers under the extended set-aside program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pulp companies, mill workers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Removing the guaranteed timber supply puts logging jobs and pulp-mill employment in southeast Alaska communities at risk, and the law responds by still requiring the Forest Service to prepare timber to meet market demand.

The conference version was much weaker than the House-passed bill: the House version required the Secretary to terminate the two pulp companies' long-term contracts within 90 days [S5], while the final law only modifies them [S8]; the House designated 23 wilderness areas [S5], the final law only 6 [S8]; and the Senate's buffer zones around all Class I and II streams [S7] were narrowed to Class I streams plus Class II streams flowing into them [S8].

The law extends the Small Business Administration set-aside program to Alaska, under which small timber purchasers can elect to have the Forest Service build the logging roads for their sales — a cost the government bears on behalf of private purchasers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The law's protections for fish streams, roadless lands, and taxpayers are real and lasting, and the annual reporting requirement exposes the program's finances to public view. But the conference process significantly diluted the original House bill: the pulp mills kept operating under modified rather than terminated contracts, most of the proposed wilderness was dropped, and the stream buffers were narrowed. The law also leaves in place a mandate to keep selling timber at market-demand levels and extends a road-building subsidy for small purchasers, so the Tongass remains a working commercial forest with public subsidies built in. On balance the public gained, but by less than the House originally voted to give it.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared both chambers by overwhelming margins, survived a House-Senate conference that softened it, and President George H.W. Bush signed it into law on November 28, 1990.

narrative.text: Introduced February 9, 1989 by Rep. Robert Mrazek, it was referred to the House Interior and Insular Affairs Committee and reported amended on June 13, 1989, then sequentially to the Agriculture Committee, which also reported it amended.
The House passed it 356–60 on July 13, 1989 (Roll Call 138).

The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee reported it with a substitute amendment on March 30, 1990, and the Senate passed it 99–0 on June 13, 1990, with all 55 Democrats and 44 of 45 Republicans voting yes.

The House disagreed with the Senate amendments and a conference committee negotiated the final version, filed October 23, 1990 as H. Rept. 101-931; the Senate and House both agreed to it in late October 1990 by voice vote.

The conference version replaced the House-passed 90-day termination of the two pulp companies' long-term contracts with required contract modifications, and reduced the wilderness designations from 23 areas to 6.
President George H.W. Bush signed it on November 28, 1990, and it became Public Law 101-626.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers, southeast Alaska fishing communities, and conservation interests gained a permanently reformed Tongass program with protected streams and roadless lands, and the annual loss-or-gain reporting requirement. The two pulp companies also came out better off than the House bill would have left them, since the final law modified their contracts instead of terminating them within 90 days and preserved a timber supply mandate to meet market demand.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, fishermen, and the pulp mills

sides.party_line_note: The fight was not between the parties: the House passed it 356–60 and the Senate 99–0, with all 55 Democrats and 44 of 45 Republicans voting yes, and a Republican president signed it. The sharpest opposition came from Alaska's own delegation, both parties.

industries.industry: Pulp and paper (Alaska Pulp Corporation and Ketchikan Pulp Company)
industries.note: The two companies lost their statutory guaranteed timber supply and saw their 50-year contracts rewritten to protect public resources and promote competition, but the conference version let the contracts continue rather than terminating them as the House bill required. Their business model had depended on cheap public timber that cost the government money and damaged fish habitat.

Logging buffer zones along fish-bearing streams protect the salmon habitat the fishing industry depends on, and the bill adds the industry as a party the Secretary must consult on forest management reports.

The law extends the SBA set-aside program to Alaska, letting small timber purchasers elect to have the Forest Service build the logging roads for their timber sales — a benefit they receive at public expense.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations (Haida, Goldbelt, Sealaska, Shee Atika, Atikon)
industries.note: The law authorizes the Haida Corporation to select withdrawn Sulzer frontage lands, trades Hobart Bay lands to Goldbelt for Echo Cove, and directs expedited negotiations for land exchanges with Sealaska, Shee Atika, and Atikon on Admiralty Island.

Wilderness and roadless designations remove lands from logging, stream buffers restrict harvest along fish streams, and the guaranteed-supply mandate is gone — though the law still requires the Forest Service to prepare timber to meet market demand.
